interview_metadata.name: Arianna Deluca
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised right here around Springtown, Texas, in a family that was very Texas on the outside and very southern Italian at the dinner table. My grandparents came to Texas in the 1920s, and by the time I came along, the stories were already family furniture: hard work, modest living, don't waste good food, and if you make something, make it with care. I was a quiet child, but not shy exactly. I liked watching people and making little stories out of what they did. My mother worked in a bank office, very neat and practical, and my father ran a small appliance repair business. I had an older brother, Marco, and a younger sister, Gina, so I learned early how to hold my place without being the loudest person in the room. I did well in school and went on to get a bachelor's degree in business at what was then North Texas State University. I did not marry and I did not have children. There were a couple of serious relationships, one in my thirties especially, but I never felt peaceful about giving up my independence. I drifted into insurance after college because I needed steady work and discovered I was good at translating complicated risk into ordinary language. Over time I built a career as an insurance sales agent in Wise County, mostly working with families, small businesses, freelancers, and lately more artists and boutique shops. Outside work, my life has been painting acrylic abstracts, playing jazz piano badly but happily, reading speculative fiction, watching the Cowboys and Astros, walking trails, gardening succulents and lavender, and keeping a home that is quiet enough for me to think.

follow_ups.question: When you picture your childhood home, what do you remember most clearly?
follow_ups.response: The kitchen table. There was always coffee, tomato sauce, somebody's bill folded under a salt shaker, and my mother telling us to clear our plates. On Sundays my grandmother would make sauce early, and the whole house smelled like garlic and basil before church.

follow_ups.question: What made insurance feel like more than just a job to you?
follow_ups.response: I realized people were afraid of what they did not understand. If I could compare a policy to layers of paint on a canvas or a fence line around a pasture, they relaxed. That moment when someone's shoulders drop and they say, now I get it, that kept me in it.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes. In my mid-thirties I had a chance to move to Dallas and take a management track job with a large insurance carrier. It would have meant better pay, a sharper title, and probably a more polished life. Around the same time, my mother was having health trouble, and I was also in a relationship with a man who expected me to fit neatly into his schedule. I remember sitting in my car outside a client's hardware store in Decatur, looking at the Dallas offer letter, and thinking, if I go, I may gain a ladder but lose my own way of working. I turned it down and stayed independent in the local market. That decision probably cost me money, but it gave me a reputation, my own client base, and a life where I could paint at night, check on family, and make my work personal. It also confirmed I was not built to be managed too tightly.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to before making that choice?
follow_ups.response: I talked to my mother, my brother Marco, and one older agent named Patsy who mentored me. Patsy told me, Arianna, you sell trust better than you sell forms, and that stuck.

follow_ups.question: What did you do the day after you turned the Dallas job down?
follow_ups.response: I drove to three client appointments, bought myself barbecue in Weatherford, and came home to paint a big red-and-black canvas. It felt like closing a gate and opening a window at the same time.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was a conscious choice. I am intuitive in the small daily things, but big life turns make me sit with a legal pad and write out what I am protecting and what I am giving up.

follow_ups.question: What was at the top of that legal pad?
follow_ups.response: Independence, family nearness, and the kind of clients I liked serving. Salary was on there too, but it was not first.

follow_ups.question: Do you still make decisions that way?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though now it may be on a yellow sticky note beside my laptop. I still write things down before I trust my gut.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A more flexible company might have helped. If that Dallas firm had offered a regional role or a mentoring path that did not require giving up my local clients, I might have considered it. Back then, women in sales over a certain age or with family obligations were expected to adapt quietly.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help in a practical way?
follow_ups.response: Patsy helped by introducing me to two small business accounts. That gave me confidence I could make up the income.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel supported by family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly. My mother worried about money, but she respected that I was choosing a life I could stand inside.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I have never been married, I am not living with a partner, and I do not have children. My family is still important, just arranged differently than some people's. My older brother Marco lives near Weatherford with his wife, and we talk every Sunday evening unless the Cowboys game has us both yelling too much to hold a sensible conversation. My younger sister Gina is in Fort Worth, and she is the one who keeps the family birthdays and holiday plans from falling apart. I have two nieces and one nephew, all grown now, and I like being the aunt who remembers what kind of books they read and slips them practical advice without making a sermon of it. My parents have both passed. I still think of them often, especially when I cook or when I catch myself using one of my father's sayings about fixing the thing in front of you before buying a new one. I am solitary by temperament, but I am not cut off. I just like relationships that have breathing room.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your siblings in person?
follow_ups.response: Marco about twice a month, usually lunch or a game on television. Gina I see every few weeks, more around holidays or if she needs help sorting insurance papers for someone.

follow_ups.question: What role do you play in the wider family?
follow_ups.response: I am the calm explainer. They call me about coverage, Medicare confusion, storm damage, and sometimes just to have someone listen without getting dramatic.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is mainly Marco, Gina, and their children now. I also have a cousin, Lucia, in Mineral Wells who feels almost like a sister because we grew up together.

follow_ups.question: How do you and Lucia stay connected?
follow_ups.response: We text recipes and church festival reminders, and we meet for coffee every month or two.

follow_ups.question: Are there any strained family relationships?
follow_ups.response: Nothing dramatic. Marco and I can argue politics, so we usually steer toward sports and food.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes. I have a small circle, not a large one. My friend Maribel walks with me on Saturday mornings when the weather behaves, and she knows every bird call before I do. Patsy, my old mentor, is retired now, but we still have lunch once a month and talk shop. There is also a little group of women from the country club tennis clinic who are not intimate friends exactly, but they are steady company in the spring. I have dated now and then, but no current romantic partner. At this age, I would rather have honest companionship than a relationship that rearranges my whole house.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Maribel usually do together?
follow_ups.response: We walk early, around 7:30, usually on a trail or quiet road, then get coffee. She brings binoculars, and I bring almonds or a thermos.

follow_ups.question: Do you socialize much after work?
follow_ups.response: Not often during the week. I may meet a client or coworker for an early supper, but most nights I want my piano, a book, or a puzzle.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Springtown, outside the busiest part, in a modest one-story brick house with a small yard and enough sun for succulents and lavender. It is a place where people notice if your trash bin stays by the road too long, sometimes kindly and sometimes nosily. There are pickup trucks, dogs barking at dusk, church signs, school traffic, and fields giving way to more subdivisions every year. I like that I can get to Weatherford or Fort Worth when I need something bigger, but my day-to-day life still feels local. My neighbors are mostly working families, retirees, and a few newer people who moved out here for space.

follow_ups.question: Who do you interact with most nearby?
follow_ups.response: My next-door neighbor, Elaine, checks mail for me when I travel. Across the street there is a young family, the Carters, and I wave to them more than I visit.

follow_ups.question: What places in town are part of your routine?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, the local pharmacy, my church, a couple of barbecue places, and the coffee shop where I sometimes meet clients before office hours.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock my doors, keep porch lights on, and pay attention, but I am not fearful. The bigger worry is traffic getting faster on roads that used to feel quiet.

follow_ups.question: Have you had any safety incidents near your home?
follow_ups.response: A few car break-ins several streets over, but nothing at my house.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for one another?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially during storms or power outages. Somebody will call or walk over if a tree limb comes down.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is familiarity. I know the roads, the rhythms, and how people talk when they are worried. The downside is that growth has made everything busier, and sometimes small-town privacy is hard to come by.

follow_ups.question: What change bothers you most?
follow_ups.response: The traffic and the feeling that land is being chopped up too quickly.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Roots, clients, family nearby, and the way the prairie sky opens up in the evening.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone. It is just me in the house full time. I have a guest room that mostly holds paintings, wrapping paper, and a half-finished jigsaw puzzle on a folding table. Family may stay for a night during bad weather or holidays, but nobody is living here with me. I like the quiet. I can practice piano at 9:00 at night or make tea at 5:30 in the morning without negotiating with anyone.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever feel lonely living alone?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, especially after a long workday, but mostly I feel restored by it.

follow_ups.question: Who has a key to your house?
follow_ups.response: My sister Gina has one, and Elaine next door has an emergency key.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. I am the only permanent household member.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been that way for years.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect it to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not unless a family emergency required it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My niece may stay one night around holidays, and Gina has stayed during ice storms, but it is occasional.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three nights in a year.

follow_ups.question: Do you host out-of-town friends?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. I am more likely to meet them somewhere.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No, just me.

follow_ups.question: Any pets away or being cared for elsewhere?
follow_ups.response: No pets right now.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays start around 5:45 or 6:00. I make coffee, water the plants if it is warm, read the news, and look at my appointments before driving to the office or to a client meeting. Mondays are usually follow-up calls and policy reviews. Tuesdays and Thursdays tend to be client-heavy, sometimes in Decatur, Weatherford, or a small shop somewhere between. Wednesdays I try to reserve for paperwork and mentoring a younger agent. Friday afternoons I clear loose ends because I hate carrying a messy list into the weekend. Saturdays are for walking, errands, painting, and sometimes tennis in spring. Sundays are church when I go, family calls, cooking something slow, and maybe an Astros game.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually stop working?
follow_ups.response: Officially around 5:30, but I often answer a client text until 7:00 if it is urgent.

follow_ups.question: What is your most consistent personal routine?
follow_ups.response: Morning coffee and evening quiet. Even if the day goes sideways, I try to sit at the piano or read before bed.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am a senior insurance sales agent. I sell and service personal and commercial policies, especially property, liability, auto, life, and small business coverage. My work is part risk assessment, part education, and part negotiation. I usually work Monday through Friday, roughly 8:30 to 5:30, but insurance does not always respect the clock. If someone has storm damage or a small business owner can only meet at 6:00, I adjust. I also do occasional Saturday morning workshops for freelancers or shop owners, maybe once every couple of months.

follow_ups.question: Where do you physically do most of your work?
follow_ups.response: A mix of the office, my car between appointments, and my home desk when I am catching up on quotes.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you like best?
follow_ups.response: The moment of making something complicated feel graspable. I like building a plan around the actual person, not just the form.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep up with my own house and yard, which is not glamorous but takes time. I volunteer at church festivals and sometimes help with community insurance workshops after storms. I check in on Patsy because she is older now, though she would fuss at me for making it sound like care. I also try to mentor two younger women in sales, usually over coffee or a phone call when they are stuck on a client situation.

follow_ups.question: How often do you mentor younger agents?
follow_ups.response: Informally every week or two. Sometimes it is a 10-minute phone call; sometimes it is lunch with notes spread across the table.

follow_ups.question: What household chore takes the most energy?
follow_ups.response: Yard work in summer. Texas heat makes even trimming lavender feel like a negotiation.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have been making myself walk more consistently because sitting in client meetings and at a screen stiffens my hips and back. I also moved more of my policy tracking into the CRM, even though I still keep handwritten notes. In the last year I cut back on evening networking events. I used to say yes automatically, but now I choose the ones that actually connect me with people I want to serve, like artists, freelancers, or small boutique owners.

follow_ups.question: What made you change the networking routine?
follow_ups.response: I got tired of collecting business cards that went nowhere. I would rather have two useful conversations than stand through a noisy mixer.

follow_ups.question: How many days a week are you walking now?
follow_ups.response: Usually four days, sometimes five if the weather is kind.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so there is not a school routine in my household. I hear about school schedules through my nieces and nephew when they were younger and through clients now. My own weekday is arranged around work appointments rather than school drop-offs or activities.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever help with nieces' or nephews' school routines?
follow_ups.response: A little. I went to school plays, helped with college forms, and occasionally picked someone up when Gina was in a bind.

follow_ups.question: Has not having children affected your work schedule?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it gave me flexibility for evening appointments, though it also meant people assumed I was always available.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited and mostly routine. I have had traffic stops, including one for speeding years ago between Springtown and Weatherford, and the officer was professional. Through work, I have dealt with police reports for auto accidents, theft claims, and storm-related property issues. In a small community you often know someone who knows the officer, so there is a familiarity, but I also understand not everyone experiences that familiarity as protection.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt mistreated by an officer?
follow_ups.response: No, not personally. I have been nervous during stops like anyone, but I have not felt mistreated.

follow_ups.question: How does your job shape your view of law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: It makes me see them as part of the paperwork chain after something goes wrong, but also as human beings under pressure.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: One that stands out was after a hailstorm when several vehicles in a church parking lot were vandalized. I helped clients collect police report numbers, and the local department was patient with older folks who were confused.

follow_ups.question: When was that?
follow_ups.response: About four years ago, in the spring after a bad storm week.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you advised clients?
follow_ups.response: It reminded me to tell people exactly what documentation to gather before they are upset and tired.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have had a distant cousin arrested for a DUI many years ago, but no close family member has been through jail or prison in a way that shaped my daily life.

follow_ups.question: Did the cousin's arrest affect the family?
follow_ups.response: It was embarrassing and worrying, but he dealt with it and quit drinking for a long time afterward.

follow_ups.question: Do clients ever discuss arrests with you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes if it affects driving records or insurance rates, but I keep that professional and private.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential, state, and local elections. I was raised that voting was one of those plain responsibilities, like paying bills and showing up when somebody is sick. I do not pretend I follow every race perfectly, but I read enough to make a decision. Local races matter to me because roads, schools, taxes, and county services affect my clients directly.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote early or on Election Day?
follow_ups.response: Usually early, because my schedule can get hijacked by client emergencies.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. I will talk issues, but I avoid turning supper into a cable news argument.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself a moderate conservative with some independent streaks. I believe in personal responsibility, small businesses, careful spending, and not making government so complicated that ordinary people cannot understand it. At the same time, I have worked with too many families and small shop owners to think everybody can just bootstrap their way through illness, disasters, or a bad economy. I support practical help when it is targeted and accountable. I am more traditional on some cultural things because of how I was raised, but I do not like cruelty dressed up as principle. I care about law and order, but I also think institutions need transparency because power can get lazy. These days I feel politically homeless sometimes. The loudest people on both sides seem to enjoy making neighbors suspicious of one another, and I do not have much patience for that.

follow_ups.question: Which issues matter most when you vote?
follow_ups.response: Small business policy, property taxes, health care costs, public safety, and whether the candidate seems grounded in real community life.

follow_ups.question: Has your work influenced those views?
follow_ups.response: Very much. Insurance teaches you that risk is real, but so is bad luck. People need incentives to be responsible, but they also need systems that do not collapse on them.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less partisan and less patient with performance politics. Ten or fifteen years ago, I probably voted Republican almost automatically. Now I still lean that way in many races, but I look harder at temperament and competence. The pandemic, health care costs, and the way people talked past each other made me rethink how much I trust party labels. I have also become more open to discussing mental health, caregiving, and older workers as policy issues, not just private family matters.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific event that pushed that change?
follow_ups.response: The pandemic was a big one. Watching small businesses struggle while people argued in slogans made me want more practical leadership.

follow_ups.question: Have family members noticed the shift?
follow_ups.response: Marco teases me that I have gone soft, but I tell him I have gone specific.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say somewhat. I am not Black, and I do not want to pretend I experience those fears directly. But the conversations made me listen more carefully, especially to clients and younger people who describe being treated differently. I also think small towns can have blind spots because people say, we know everybody here, when really they may only know people like themselves. The movement did not change every belief I have about policing, but it made the issue harder for me to dismiss.

follow_ups.question: Did you hear personal stories from anyone you know?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a younger Black client told me how anxious he gets during traffic stops. He said it plainly, and I remembered it.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your conversations locally?
follow_ups.response: It made me less quick to accept easy answers. I ask more questions now before stating an opinion.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the central issue is whether people are treated with equal dignity and whether public power is accountable. I do not agree with every slogan or every tactic associated with the movement, but I do think it raised real concerns about excessive force, profiling, and whose pain gets believed. My instinct is reform more than tearing institutions down. Better training, clearer reporting, consequences for misconduct, and community relationships seem practical to me. I also think people need to be able to discuss police safety and racial fairness in the same sentence.

follow_ups.question: What kind of reforms sound reasonable to you?
follow_ups.response: Body cameras used properly, transparent complaint processes, de-escalation training, and departments not protecting bad officers.

follow_ups.question: What makes the conversation hard?
follow_ups.response: People treat any nuance as betrayal. If you support accountability, some say you hate police; if you support police safety, others say you ignore racism.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race remains woven into opportunity in ways some of us were not taught to see. I grew up hearing immigrant stories from my Italian family, and those stories were about hardship, but they were not the same as the history Black Americans carry. I have been trying to hold both truths: my family worked hard, and other families faced barriers mine did not face in the same way. In business, I notice who gets assumed competent, who gets second chances, and who has to explain themselves more. I am still learning, but I am more aware than I used to be.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Mostly long-form articles, interviews, church discussions, and conversations with people I know rather than social media fights.

follow_ups.question: Does your Italian background affect how you think about it?
follow_ups.response: It gives me sympathy for immigrant struggle, but I have had to learn not to use that as a shortcut for understanding everybody else's history.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked in small settings with family, friends, church people, and a few clients when it came up naturally. I have not joined protests. I try to listen more than perform my opinion.

follow_ups.question: Have any conversations been difficult?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with Marco. He gets defensive quickly, so I try to bring it back to specific stories instead of slogans.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any behavior?
follow_ups.response: I pay more attention to whose voices are in the room and whose concerns get brushed aside.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: It varies. My sister Gina is fairly open and tends to worry about fairness, especially in schools and health care. Marco is more skeptical and thinks the media exaggerates things. Maribel is very thoughtful and has pushed me to read more carefully. My work circle is mixed, so people often avoid the topic unless they already know where everyone stands. I would say most people close to me are aware of the issue, but not many are activists.

follow_ups.question: Do these differences strain relationships?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but we usually recover because we have shared history and practical things to do together.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you most on this topic?
follow_ups.response: Probably Maribel and a few younger clients. They made it personal without turning it into a lecture.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is decent for 62. I have some stiffness in my hips and lower back if I sit too long, and my doctor watches my cholesterol and blood pressure. I am not an athlete, but I walk, play low-impact tennis in spring, and try to keep my weight reasonable. I wear reading glasses and I am careful on uneven trails. My energy is best in the morning and drops after about 8:30 at night.

follow_ups.question: Do you take regular medications?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a low-dose blood pressure medication and a statin for cholesterol.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Twice a year unless something comes up.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when my routine is steady and the weather allows walking. It is hard when work piles up, because I snack on pretzels, eat late brisket tacos, and sit too much. I enjoy good food, especially steak and Italian cooking, so moderation is my lifelong negotiation. Having walking friends helps because I am more likely to show up if Maribel is waiting.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Morning walks and keeping fruit, almonds, and yogurt in the house.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest to break?
follow_ups.response: Salty evening snacks while watching cooking shows.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing catastrophic. About a year ago my doctor became firmer about my blood pressure, so I started medication and got more serious about walking. I had a flare of lower back pain after moving boxes in my garage, and physical therapy gave me stretches I actually do most mornings. I also had a skin spot removed from my shoulder that turned out benign, but it scared me enough to wear sunscreen more faithfully.

follow_ups.question: How did physical therapy fit into your schedule?
follow_ups.response: I went early twice a week for about six weeks before work.

follow_ups.question: Did the blood pressure diagnosis worry you?
follow_ups.response: A little. It made aging feel less theoretical, but it also gave me something concrete to manage.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working, but back pain can slow me down. If I have several long drives and meetings in one day, I have to stretch or I get stiff and irritable.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Only a few half-days for appointments or when my back was flaring.

follow_ups.question: Do clients know about it?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. I may joke about needing to stand up, but I keep it light.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. My mother's later years involved heart trouble and diabetes, and I helped with appointments and paperwork. More recently, Patsy had a knee replacement, and I drove her to a couple of follow-ups. Gina had a breast cancer scare that turned out okay, but the weeks of waiting were hard on all of us. I am often the person who can translate insurance or medical bills, so loved ones bring me the confusing envelopes.

follow_ups.question: How much caregiving are you doing now?
follow_ups.response: Not daily caregiving, mostly check-ins, rides now and then, and paperwork help.

follow_ups.question: Does that feel burdensome?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I would rather be useful than stand by helplessly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I am fortunate to have employer-sponsored health insurance, and because of my work I understand networks and deductibles better than most. Even so, it is frustrating. Appointments take time, specialists are not always close, and you can still get a bill that makes no sense. I have delayed dental work before because it was expensive, but I have not gone without major medical care. For family, the hardest part is explaining Medicare supplements and what is actually covered.

transcript.response: Yes, she worked for pay.

follow_ups.response: Mostly part time when we were young, then closer to full time later.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect household routines?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we all had chores.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked as a bank teller and later in bookkeeping support. She handled deposits, customer questions, account records, and the kind of careful paperwork that requires patience. She was good with numbers and calm with people.

follow_ups.question: Did she teach you money habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Balance the account, keep receipts, and do not spend money twice in your mind.

follow_ups.question: Did her work influence your career?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she showed me that trust and accuracy matter in financial conversations.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a local community bank. They handled checking and savings accounts, small loans, farm and household banking, and basic financial services for local families and businesses.

follow_ups.question: Was it a big institution?
follow_ups.response: No, it felt local. Customers recognized the staff.

follow_ups.question: Did you visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, and I remember how quiet and orderly it seemed.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked for pay throughout my childhood.

follow_ups.question: Was he self-employed?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for much of it.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when repairs backed up.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father repaired appliances and later ran a small repair shop. He fixed washers, refrigerators, ovens, and whatever else people hauled in. His most important duties were diagnosing problems, ordering parts, making service calls, and treating customers fairly enough that they came back.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from watching him?
follow_ups.response: Start with the actual problem, not the fanciest solution.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you repairs?
follow_ups.response: A little. I can troubleshoot simple things, though I am no mechanic.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked in a small local appliance repair business, first for someone else and then his own shop. They did not manufacture anything; they repaired household machines and made service calls to farms, homes, and small businesses.

follow_ups.question: Was the business part of the community?
follow_ups.response: Yes. People knew my father by name and trusted him in their homes.

follow_ups.question: Did money feel secure growing up?
follow_ups.response: Modest, not luxurious, but steady enough if we were careful.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am still useful, but less rushed. I would like to be either running a small boutique insurance practice or consulting niche focused on artists, freelancers, and small businesses that need someone imaginative and careful. I want to mentor women in sales over 50 because I know how easy it is for industries to treat experience as if it expires. I would like to make real progress on my guide, Imaginative Insurance: How Artful Thinking Improves Risk Management, even if it begins as workshops and essays. Personally, I hope to travel more in off-peak seasons, return to Santa Fe, take that Kyoto garden trip if finances allow, and keep my health strong enough for walking trails and low-impact tennis. I do not need a flashy life. I want a textured one, with color, purpose, good meals, honest work, and enough quiet to hear myself think.

follow_ups.question: What is the first practical step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Building a list of clients in creative fields and testing a workshop series for them.

follow_ups.question: What do you hope stays exactly the same?
follow_ups.response: My independence, my family ties, and the feeling of coming home to a quiet house with paint drying in the corner.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value integrity, independence, craft, family loyalty, and imagination. Integrity because people trust me with fearful parts of their lives. Independence because I know myself best when I have room to choose. Craft because whether it is a policy, a painting, a repair, or a meal, the way you make something matters. Family loyalty does not mean living in each other's pockets; it means answering the phone. And imagination keeps life from becoming only bills, forms, and appointments.

follow_ups.question: Which value did your parents teach most strongly?
follow_ups.response: Craft and responsibility. Do the work right, and do not make someone chase you for what you owe.

follow_ups.question: Which value feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Imagination. It is how I turn ordinary work into something alive.
